X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Home Body-Fat Analyser
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two product descriptions: (A) a premium, branded home body-fat analyser marketed for personal health monitoring; (B) a niche-branded home body-fat analyser marketed for athletes and fitness enthusiasts. Both descriptions include price points (e.g., €250 for premium, €150 for niche) and a brief product description. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 0‑10 scale and
X1.sample: 500 adults aged 25‑55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region (Japan, US, Europe).
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (0‑10) for each product description.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium product will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than the niche product (difference ≥ 1.5 points).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Niche product will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than the premium product (difference ≥ 1.5 points).

X1.decision_rule: If premium product mean ≥ niche product mean + 1.5 points, proceed with premium consumer proposition. If niche product mean ≥ premium product mean + 1.5 points, proceed with niche athlete proposition. If difference < 1.5 points, inconclusive; consider

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or adoption of a home body-fat analyser. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on B2B markets and existing product lines. Conduct a targeted survey test (as proposed) to empirically compare purchase intent for a premium, branded home body-fat analyser versus a niche-branded athlete version before any larger investment.
final.target_customer: Individual health-conscious consumers seeking personal health monitoring (T1) and fitness enthusiasts/athletes seeking performance data (T2).
final.value_proposition: Premium, branded home body-fat analyser for personal health monitoring (T1) and niche-branded athlete version for performance tracking (T2).
final.next_action: Run the proposed consumer preference survey (500 participants, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent for premium versus niche versions.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and actual sales of a consumer product.
would_change_if: If the survey shows premium product purchase intent ≥ niche + 1.5 points, proceed with premium consumer proposition.
If niche product intent ≥ premium + 1.5 points, proceed with niche athlete proposition.
If both scores are within 1.5 points of each other, results are inconclusive and further testing is needed.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed PLB Purchase Intent Survey (test X1) to empirically test whether outdoor recreationists will adopt the device for safety reasons. If the survey confirms willingness to pay ≥$300 and purchase intent ≥40% among outdoor recreationists, proceed with a limited consumer launch; otherwise, maintain the current B2B focus.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, paddlers) who participate in activities in remote locations and value safety.
final.value_proposition: A reliable, FCC-compliant 406 MHz distress beacon that reduces search and rescue time and provides peace of mind for outdoor enthusiasts.
final.next_action: Run the PLB Purchase Intent Survey (test X1) within the 12‑week timeline and €15,000 budget.
final.uncertainty: The actual purchase intent of outdoor recreationists for a 406 MHz PLB is unknown; evidence of successful rescues and regulatory approval do not prove demand.
would_change_if: If the survey shows willingness to pay ≥$300 and purchase intent ≥40% among outdoor recreationists, the favoured theory would shift to likely and investment would proceed.

T1.who_benefits: Hikers, campers, and other outdoor users who face high risk of isolation and need rapid SAR response.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Legal requirement for registration and mandatory use in remote environments creates a compliance-driven demand; users trust devices that have proven track record of saving lives.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can charge a premium for a certified, reliable device that meets regulatory standards, and sell through outdoor retailers and emergency services.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in the U.S. is large and growing in 2002.
Search and rescue agencies will prioritize devices that meet the new FCC standard.
Consumers are willing to pay a price premium for safety certification.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor enthusiasts will indicate willingness to purchase a 406 MHz PLB at a price above $300.
Adoption rates will be higher in states with mandatory registration laws.
Survival rates for hikers with PLBs will be statistically higher than without.

T2.who_benefits: Search and rescue agencies, national parks, outdoor recreation organizations, and government safety departments that need reliable, traceable distress devices.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Legal requirement for mandatory registration and use in remote areas drives procurement; agencies prioritize devices that meet the new standard to avoid fines and improve operational efficiency.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell through government contracts and emergency service channels at higher margins, and potentially license the technology to other manufacturers for B2B distribution.
assumptions: Government and public safety budgets for search and rescue are sufficient to purchase certified devices.
Compliance with FCC rules is enforced and monitored.
Outdoor organizations and parks have procurement processes that include technology evaluation.
predictions: Government procurement requests for 406 MHz PLBs will increase after the FCC ruling.
Adoption rates will be higher in regions with active search and rescue programs and large outdoor recreation areas.
Cost savings from faster search times will be documented in case studies.

X1.name: Consumer vs Government Demand Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor activity forums and clubs) and (B) Emergency services/outdoor organizations (recruited via SAR agency and park management contacts). Both groups view a product description of the 406 MHz PLB highlighting compliance, reliability, and survival benefits. Group A is asked: "Would you purchase this device for personal outdoor use at a price of $350?" Group B is asked: "Would you purchase this device for your organization at a price of $450, with a 10% discount for bulk orders?" Both groups are also asked about their current use of distress beacons and their awareness of the new FCC registration requirement.
X1.sample: 200 participants: 100 outdoor enthusiasts (Group A) and 100 emergency/outdoor organization representatives (Group B). Recruitment cost €2,000 (estimated).
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" vs "Would not buy") and willingness to pay (price sensitivity).

prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B purchase intent ≥50% and willingness to pay ≥$450; Group A purchase intent <30% because emergency services and organizations are the primary target.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A purchase intent ≥50% AND Group B purchase intent <30%, proceed with consumer-focused proposition (supports T1). final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct a targeted pilot test (e.g., the proposed consumer vs government demand survey) to validate demand before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (Group A) and emergency services/outdoor organizations (Group B) as identified in the test.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition would emphasize the 406 MHz distress beacon’s survival benefits and compliance advantage for outdoor users. A B2B/government proposition would emphasize the same benefits for search and rescue agencies,
final.next_action: Run the proposed consumer vs government demand survey (200 participants, €2,000 budget, 12 weeks) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for each group.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to limited evidence of actual consumer demand and market size. The survey will resolve this.
would_change_if: If Group A purchase intent ≥50% and willingness to pay ≥$350, T1 becomes likely and the consumer proposition is justified.
If Group B purchase intent ≥50% and willingness to pay ≥$450, T2 becomes likely and the B2B/government proposition is justified.
If both groups show ≥30% intent, both theories remain uncertain and further testing is needed.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, technical feasibility, and potential value capture.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be established.
Evidence must be from sources published on or before late 2002; later developments cannot be used.
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness, marine tourism) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
Expand the existing B2B product line into new customer segments (e.g., recreational boats, private aircraft) without creating a distinct consumer proposition.
Maintain the current product portfolio and distribution channels (no expansion).
License the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology to third parties for consumer applications, rather than developing a proprietary consumer product.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they reduce search time and increase survival probability, leading to willingness to pay a premium price for a differentiated consumer proposition.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Evidence shows PLBs have saved lives and improved SAR efficiency; users value a device that works in remote areas and can be used by non-experts.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can charge a premium for a branded, easy-to-use consumer product, sell through outdoor retailers, and potentially license the technology to other outdoor brands.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in the U.S. is large and growing in 2002.
PLBs are perceived as a safety necessity rather than a luxury.
Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that is clearly marketed for outdoor use and complies with regulations.
predictions: In a test offering a branded outdoor-focused PLB at a price 20% above standard PLBs, purchase intent among outdoor recreation users will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a generic PLB.

predictions: In a test offering a branded PLB marketed as a compliance product at a price 15% above standard PLBs, purchase intent among safety-conscious consumers will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for a generic PLB.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, technical feasibility, and potential value capture.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be established.
Evidence must be from sources published on or before late 2002; later developments cannot be used.
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness, marine tourism) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
Expand the existing B2B product line into new customer segments (e.g., recreational boats, private aircraft) without creating a distinct consumer proposition.
Maintain the current product portfolio and distribution channels (no expansion).
License the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology to third parties for consumer applications, rather than developing a proprietary consumer product.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, emergency-proven safety solution that can be used in remote, high-risk environments.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor recreation users (hikers, campers, paddlers) who need a device that can be used when other communication methods fail.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The FCC legalizing PLBs in 2002 and the documented rescues (e.g., 230 outdoor enthusiasts saved) create a perceived safety benefit; users trust a device that has proven its ability to summon help.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can charge a premium price for a specialized outdoor PLB, sell through outdoor retailers and outdoor activity clubs, and potentially bundle with other safety gear.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in the U.S. is large enough to support a dedicated consumer product.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for safety-proven outdoor gear.
Distribution channels (retailers, clubs) exist to reach this segment.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreation users will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz PLB at a price above $200.
Sales of a dedicated outdoor PLB will be positively correlated with outdoor recreation participation rates.
Adoption will be higher in regions with high outdoor activity levels.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline are analyst assumptions for evaluating evidence.
Evidence must address consumer behavior, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape, not just product capability.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, hobby gardening, or a niche agricultural task) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing consumer offering by introducing a new model or line that serves the same broad market without differentiation (e.g., a basic tractor for small‑holders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the existing B2B dealer network and existing product lines without new consumer propositions.
4) License tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications, leveraging Deere’s engineering without direct consumer sales.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment.
T1.who_benefits: Households with small gardens and limited storage space who need a versatile tool for various yard tasks.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. A single, compact tractor that can perform several tasks reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.
assumptions: Small‑holder households have limited budget for multiple specialized tools.
Versatility is a primary purchase criterion for these consumers.
Deere can engineer a compact tractor that performs multiple tasks without compromising durability.
predictions: In a test offering a multi‑purpose tractor at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, purchase intent among small‑holder respondents will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor.
Surveyed willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose tractor will be at least 10% higher than for a comparable single‑purpose model.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline are analyst assumptions for evaluating evidence.
Evidence must address consumer behavior, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape, not just product capability.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, hobby gardening, or a niche agricultural task) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing consumer offering by introducing a new model or line that serves the same broad market without differentiation (e.g., a basic tractor for small‑holders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the existing B2B dealer network and existing product lines without new consumer propositions.
4) License tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications, leveraging Deere’s engineering without direct consumer sales.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment.
T1.who_benefits: Households with small gardens and limited storage space who need a versatile tool for various yard tasks.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. A single, compact tractor that can perform several tasks reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.
assumptions: Small‑holder households have limited budget for multiple specialized tools.
Versatility is a primary purchase criterion for these consumers.
Deere can engineer a compact tractor that performs multiple tasks without compromising durability.
predictions: In a test offering a multi‑purpose tractor at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, purchase intent among small‑holder respondents will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor.
Surveyed willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose tractor will be at least 10% higher than for a comparable single‑purpose model.

assumptions: Status is a primary purchase driver for a segment of small‑holder households.
Modern, aesthetically pleasing design is valued over purely functional features.
Deere can design a tractor that is visually distinctive without compromising performance.
predictions: In a test offering a status‑oriented tractor at a price above comparable functional models, purchase intent among affluent respondents will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for a purely functional tractor.
Willingness to pay for a status‑oriented tractor will be at least 15% higher than for a comparable functional model.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to empirically test whether a functional, multi‑purpose tractor meets purchase intent and willingness‑to‑pay thresholds. If the survey confirms the functional model, proceed to develop a differentiated functional consumer proposition; otherwise, reconsider or abandon the consumer expansion.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline are analyst assumptions for evaluating evidence.
Evidence must address consumer behavior, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape, not just product capability.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, hobby gardening, or a niche agricultural task) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing consumer offering by introducing a new model or line that serves the same broad market without differentiation (e.g., a basic tractor for small‑holders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the existing B2B dealer network and existing product lines without new consumer propositions.
4) License tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications, leveraging Deere’s engineering without direct consumer sales.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment.
T1.who_benefits: Households with small gardens and limited storage space who need a versatile tool for various yard tasks.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. A single, compact tractor that can perform several tasks reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.
assumptions: Small‑holder households have limited budget for multiple specialized tools.
Versatility is a primary purchase criterion for these consumers.
Deere can engineer a compact tractor that performs multiple tasks without compromising durability.
predictions: In a test offering a multi‑purpose tractor at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, purchase intent among small‑holder respondents will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor.
Surveyed willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose tractor will be at least 10% higher than for a comparable single‑purpose model.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a status symbol and status-driven purchase, because they associate the tractor with modern, affluent lifestyle and community recognition.
T2.who_benefits: Affluent households and early adopters who use lawn care as a way to signal social status and modern living.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers seek products that convey prestige and align with their social circle. A tractor that is marketed as a stylish, innovative tool becomes a visible marker of affluence.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price the tractor at a premium, sell branded apparel and accessories, and build a community around ownership, creating a lifestyle brand that commands higher margins.
assumptions: Status is a primary purchase driver for a segment of small‑holder households.
Modern, aesthetically pleasing design is valued over purely functional features.
Deere can design a tractor that is visually distinctive without compromising performance.
predictions: In a test offering a status‑oriented tractor at a price above comparable functional models, purchase intent among affluent respondents will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for a purely functional tractor.
Willingness to pay for a status‑oriented tractor will be at least 15% higher than for a comparable functional model.
T2.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a status symbol and status-driven purchase, because they associate the tractor with modern, affluent lifestyle and community recognition.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractor
X1.method: Online survey with randomized product presentation. Participants view two tractor concepts: a functional, multi‑purpose model (one compact tractor performing multiple tasks) and a status‑oriented model (same tractor styled with modern aesthetic, premium pricing). They are asked about willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (binary).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. households with small gardens (under 1/4 acre) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and region.
X1.measure: 1) WTP: maximum price participants would pay for each tractor concept. 2) Purchase intent: percentage indicating "Very likely" to buy each concept. 3) Secondary: perceived practicality (1‑10 scale) and perceived status (1‑10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Functional tractor will show higher WTP and purchase intent than status tractor, with a difference of at least 10 percentage points in purchase intent and a WTP premium of at least 10%.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Status tractor will show higher WTP and purchase intent than functional tractor, with a difference of at least 10 percentage points in purchase intent and a WTP premium of at least 15%.

X1.decision_rule: If functional tractor meets both WTP and purchase intent thresholds (e.g., purchase intent ≥ 35% and WTP ≥ $2,500) and status tractor does not meet either threshold, proceed with a differentiated functional consumer proposition. If status tractor meets both thresholds and functional tractor does not, proceed with a differentiated status‑oriented consumer proposition. If neither meets thresholds,

final.value_proposition: A compact, multi‑purpose lawn and garden tractor that performs several tasks (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) without compromising durability, offering a single reliable machine that reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, hobby gardening, or a niche agricultural task) using existing tractor engineering.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractor
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized product presentation. Participants view two tractor concepts: a functional, multi‑purpose model (one compact tractor performing multiple tasks) and a status‑oriented model (same tractor styled with modern aesthetic, premium pricing). They are asked about willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (binary).
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. households with small gardens (under 1/4 acre) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and region.
arguments.measure: 1) WTP: maximum price participants would pay for each tractor concept. 2) Purchase intent: percentage indicating "Very likely" to buy each concept. 3) Secondary: perceived practicality (1‑10 scale) and perceived status (1‑10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Functional tractor will show higher WTP and purchase intent than status tractor, with a difference of at least 10 percentage points in purchase intent and a WTP premium of at least 10%.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Status tractor will show higher WTP and purchase intent than functional tractor, with a difference of at least 10 percentage points in purchase intent and a WTP premium of at least 15%.

arguments.decision_rule: If functional tractor meets both WTP and purchase intent thresholds (e.g., purchase intent ≥ 35% and WTP ≥ $2,500) and status tractor does not meet either threshold, proceed with a differentiated functional consumer proposition. If status tractor meets both thresholds and functional tractor does not, proceed with a differentiated status‑oriented consumer proposition. If neither meets thresholds,

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to empirically test whether a functional, multi‑purpose tractor meets purchase intent and willingness‑to‑pay thresholds. If the survey confirms the functional model, proceed to develop a differentiated functional consumer proposition; otherwise, reconsider or abandon the consumer expansion.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline are analyst assumptions for evaluating evidence.
Evidence must address consumer behavior, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape, not just product capability.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, hobby gardening, or a niche agricultural task) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing consumer offering by introducing a new model or line that serves the same broad market without differentiation (e.g., a basic tractor for small‑holders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the existing B2B dealer network and existing product lines without new consumer propositions.
4) License tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications, leveraging Deere’s engineering without direct consumer sales.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment.
T1.who_benefits: Households with small gardens and limited storage space who need a versatile tool for various yard tasks.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. A single, compact tractor that can perform several tasks reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.
assumptions: Small‑holder households have limited budget for multiple specialized tools.
Versatility is a primary purchase criterion for these consumers.
Deere can engineer a compact tractor that performs multiple tasks without compromising durability.
predictions: In a test offering a multi‑purpose tractor at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, purchase intent among small‑holder respondents will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor.
Surveyed willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose tractor will be at least 10% higher than for a comparable single‑purpose model.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a status symbol and status-driven purchase, because they associate the tractor with modern, affluent lifestyle and community recognition.
T2.who_benefits: Affluent households and early adopters who use lawn care as a way to signal social status and modern living.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers seek products that convey prestige and align with their social circle. A tractor that is marketed as a stylish, innovative tool becomes a visible marker of affluence.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price the tractor at a premium, sell branded apparel and accessories, and build a community around ownership, creating a lifestyle brand that commands higher margins.
assumptions: Status is a primary purchase driver for a segment of small‑holder households.
Modern, aesthetically pleasing design is valued over purely functional features.
Deere can design a tractor that is visually distinctive without compromising performance.
predictions: In a test offering a status‑oriented tractor at a price above comparable functional models, purchase intent among affluent respondents will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for a purely functional tractor.
Willingness to pay for a status‑oriented tractor will be at least 15% higher than for a comparable functional model.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized product presentation. Participants view two tractor concepts: a functional, multi‑purpose model (one compact tractor performing multiple tasks) and a status‑oriented model (same tractor styled with modern aesthetic, premium pricing). X1.sample: 500 U.S. households with small gardens (under 1/4 acre) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and region.
X1.measure: 1) WTP: maximum price participants would pay for each tractor concept. 2) Purchase intent: percentage indicating "Very likely" to buy each concept. 3) Secondary: perceived practicality (1‑10 scale) and perceived status (1‑10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T2: Status tractor will show higher WTP and purchase intent than functional tractor, with a difference of at least 10 percentage points in purchase intent and a WTP premium of at least 15%.

X1.decision_rule: If functional tractor meets both WTP and purchase intent thresholds (e.g., purchase intent ≥ 35% and WTP ≥ $2,500) and status tractor does not meet either threshold, proceed with a differentiated functional consumer proposition. If status tractor meets both thresholds and functional tractor does not, proceed with a differentiated status‑oriented consumer proposition. If neither meets thresholds,

final.value_proposition: A compact, multi‑purpose lawn and garden tractor that performs several tasks (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) without compromising durability, offering a single reliable machine that reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.
